5790: The serpent (Hebrew nachash), "more crafty than any other beast of the field". Genesis itself does not call it Satan; the identification is made explicitly in Rev 12:9 and 20:2 ("that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan") and is assumed in Second Temple texts such as Wisdom of Solomon 2:24.
5791: The serpent questions God's word and tells the woman she will "be like God (or gods), knowing good and evil". The humans eat, are expelled from the garden, and lose access to the tree of life; cherubim guard the way back. Heiser suggests nachash carries a triple wordplay: "serpent", "diviner" (from the verb nachash, to practise divination, Gen 44:5) and "shining one" (linked to nechoshet, bronze; compare Num 21:9). Most lexicons and commentators accept only "serpent" as the meaning here and regard the wordplay as possible but unproven. Some (Heiser among them) link the scene with Ezek 28:13-17, where a figure "in Eden, the garden of God", an "anointed guardian cherub", is cast down for pride; the passage is addressed to the king of Tyre, and the Hebrew and Greek even differ over whether the king is the cherub or was with the cherub.
5792: Death and exile from God's presence for humankind; a curse on the serpent, who is cast down to "eat dust" (a common image for humiliation and the underworld); and lasting hostility between the serpent's offspring and the woman's.
5793: Gen 3:15 promises that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head while being struck on the heel; Christians from Irenaeus on call it the "first gospel" (protoevangelium). Paul promises that God "will soon crush Satan under your feet" (Rom 16:20); the cross disarms the powers (Col 2:15); Revelation shows the dragon thrown down and finally thrown into the lake of fire (Rev 12:9; 20:10), and the tree of life is open again (Rev 22:2).
5795: The serpent is Satan or his instrument; this has been the standard Christian and much Jewish reading since the Second Temple period, building on Rev 12:9 and John 8:44 ("a murderer from the beginning").
5797: The nachash is a member of God's heavenly household, a throne guardian who resented humans being made God's image-bearers and turned them against God. Ezek 28 and Isa 14 are read as echoing this primal fall.
5799: Many critical scholars read the serpent as simply a clever animal in a story about human disobedience, the origin of mortality and why snakes crawl; the link to Satan is a later development. Jewish interpretation varies, often stressing the human evil inclination over a cosmic adversary.
5800: The sons of God and the Nephilim
5801: "The sons of God" (bene ha-elohim) who "saw that the daughters of man were attractive" and took wives; the Nephilim ("fallen ones" or possibly "giants") who were on the earth "in those days, and also afterward", the "mighty men of old, men of renown".
5802: In four compressed verses, the sons of God take human wives; God limits human life to 120 years; the Nephilim are mentioned; and the flood story begins with the world's wickedness (Gen 6:5). The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 6–16, probably third century BC) expands this: 200 angelic "Watchers" led by Shemihazah swear an oath on Mount Hermon, marry women, teach forbidden arts (weapons, sorcery, astrology), and father giants who devour the earth. Jude 1:6 and 2 Pet 2:4 (which uses the Greek verb for consigning to Tartarus) refer to angels who sinned, left their proper dwelling and are kept in chains until judgment, and Jude 1:14-15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9, so most scholars think these letters know the Enochic story. Nephilim reappear in the spies' report about Canaan (Num 13:33), linked with the Anakim and Rephaim (Deut 2:10-11; Deut 3:11).
5803: The spread of violence and corruption that leads to the flood (Gen 6:5-13); in the Enochic tradition, the imprisonment of the Watchers and the release of evil spirits from the giants' bodies (1 Enoch 15:8-12). In the biblical text, the later giant clans of Canaan who must be faced in the conquest.
5804: On the council reading, the imprisoned spirits are those to whom Christ "proclaimed" his victory (1 Pet 3:19-20, read with 1 Enoch), and the angels who sinned are kept for judgment, which believers will share (1 Cor 6:3). Others read 1 Pet 3:19 as Christ preaching through Noah to people of Noah's day, or as a descent to the dead; the passage is one of the most debated in the New Testament.
5806: The sons of God are heavenly beings, as the phrase means in Job 1:6, 2:1 and 38:7. This is the oldest attested reading: 1 Enoch, Jubilees, the Dead Sea Scrolls, Josephus (*Antiquities* 1.73) and Philo (who allegorises it), and early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr (*2 Apology* 5), Athenagoras, Irenaeus and Tertullian. Most modern critical scholars (e.g. Ronald Hendel) and many evangelicals hold it. Objection: Jesus says angels "neither marry nor are given in marriage" (Matt 22:30); reply: he speaks of angels "in heaven", not of fallen ones who left their proper place (Jude 1:6).
5808: The "sons of God" are the godly line of Seth (Gen 4:26; Gen 5) who intermarried with the ungodly line of Cain; the sin is religious compromise. It appears in Christian writing with Julius Africanus (early third century), was taken up by Ephrem, John Chrysostom and others, and became dominant in the West after Augustine (*City of God* 15.23), who thought angels could not father children; Luther and Calvin held it. Strengths: the passage is about human wickedness and judgment falls on humans. Critics note that Genesis never calls Seth's line "sons of God" and that "daughters of man" naturally means women generally.
5810: The sons of God are kings or nobles (ancient kings were called sons of a god) who took women by force, perhaps building harems, and became tyrants ("men of renown"). Jewish tradition from the second century AD onward favoured readings like this: Targum Onkelos renders "sons of the great ones", and Genesis Rabbah 26.5 reports Rabbi Simeon bar Yohai cursing anyone who called them "sons of God" (meaning angels). Defended in modern times by Meredith Kline and others. Critics ask why the offspring would be singled out as Nephilim.
5811: Babel and the allotment of the nations
5812: The people of Shinar (Babylonia), building a city and a tower "with its top in the heavens", probably a ziggurat, a stepped temple-tower meant to link earth and heaven. On the council reading, also the heavenly beings to whom the scattered nations were then allotted.
5813: Humanity, told to fill the earth (Gen 9:1), instead gathers to "make a name for ourselves". Yahweh comes down, confuses their language and scatters them, and the city is called Babel (a pun on balal, "confuse"). Genesis 10 lists the resulting seventy nations. In Deut 32:8-9 (in its older form) the Most High divides the nations according to the number of the sons of God, but keeps Jacob as his portion; Deut 4:19-20 says the sun, moon and stars were "allotted to all the peoples" whereas Yahweh took Israel for himself.
5814: On the council reading, the nations are disinherited: given over to lesser gods who then demand worship and rule unjustly (Deut 32:17; Ps 82:2-5), which is why Israel is forbidden to worship the "host of heaven" and why Daniel sees angelic "princes" of Persia and Greece. On other readings, the consequence is simply the scattering of humankind into rival nations and languages, each falling into idolatry.
5815: God immediately calls Abraham, through whom "all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (Gen 12:3). At Pentecost the Spirit enables the apostles to speak in the languages of the nations, and Peter's hearers come from a long list of peoples (Acts 2:1-11); Paul tells the Athenians that God fixed the nations' boundaries so that they might seek him (Acts 17:26-27). Revelation ends with a great multitude "from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages" before the throne (Rev 7:9).
5817: Babel is a third rebellion: God judges it by giving the nations over to the sons of God, like handing people over to what they want (compare Rom 1:24). The gods of the nations are real but subordinate beings, and the rest of the Bible is about Yahweh taking the nations back. Held by Heiser and, in various forms, by many who accept the Qumran reading; it draws on wider studies of ancient "national gods" such as Daniel Block's *The Gods of the Nations* (1988).
5819: Augustine (*City of God* 16.4-11) read Babel as the pride of the earthly city, which God humbled, while the City of God continued through Shem and Eber to Abraham. The classical view also generally held that angels watch over nations (a view traceable to Dan 10 and found in Origen and Pseudo-Dionysius) but without the idea that the nations' gods were the appointed angels gone bad.
5821: Babel is a story explaining the variety of languages and mocking Babylon's ziggurats; Deut 32:8-9 preserves an older Israelite picture in which El Elyon (the Most High) gave each nation to one of his sons, Yahweh receiving Israel, before Yahweh and El were fully identified (Mark Smith and others). Many scholars dispute that the verse ever distinguished Yahweh from Elyon.
5823: Humanity's united rebellion ends with languages confused and peoples scattered into the seventy nations of Genesis 10. On the divine-council reading, the nations are also placed under the oversight of the sons of God; on other readings they simply drift into idolatry.
5825: Immediately after Babel, God calls one man out of Mesopotamia and promises that "in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed". Paul calls this promise "the gospel preached beforehand to Abraham". The plan for the nations begins with one family.
5827: Israel is Yahweh's "portion" and "allotted heritage", a "kingdom of priests" set among the nations. A priest stands between God and others, so Israel's calling was always meant to serve the wider world, not only itself.
5829: The prophets speak to and about the nations: Jeremiah is a "prophet to the nations", Amos announces judgment on Israel's neighbours, Jonah preaches in Nineveh, and Isaiah foresees the nations streaming to Zion and even Egypt and Assyria called God's people alongside Israel.
5831: "Arise, O God, judge the earth; for you shall inherit all the nations." Isaiah expects God to punish "the host of heaven in heaven, and the kings of the earth on the earth", and Daniel sees dominion over all nations given to one like a son of man. Council readers call Ps 82:8 the thesis of the whole biblical story; others see it as one strong strand among several.
5833: Jesus says the "ruler of this world" is being cast out; Paul says that at the cross God "disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame", and that the risen Christ sits "far above all rule and authority". Then the risen Jesus, now holding "all authority in heaven and on earth", sends his disciples to "all nations".
5835: At Pentecost the Spirit gives speech in many languages, and Jews from across the known world hear God's works "in our own tongues". That Pentecost undoes Babel is an ancient and widely shared Christian reading. That Luke's list of peoples (Acts 2:9-11) was deliberately modelled on the Table of Nations in Gen 10 (argued by James M. Scott and others) is a hypothesis; many scholars think the list reflects the Jewish diaspora of Luke's day or an astrological geography instead.
5837: Paul preaches "from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum" and plans to go on to Spain. Isaiah had foreseen messengers sent to the far nations, including Tarshish (probably in Spain), to declare God's glory. Some scholars (James M. Scott, Roger Aus, and popularly Heiser) suggest Paul was consciously working through the Table of Nations or Isaiah 66 toward the western edge of the world. This is an attractive hypothesis but Paul never says so; he gives practical reasons too (Rom 15:20-24). Whether he reached Spain is unknown; 1 Clement 5.7 says he went to "the limit of the west".
5838: The powers subjected and the church as witness
5839: Through the church "the manifold wisdom of God" is made known "to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places"; Christ must reign until every rule, authority and power is subjected and every knee bows. On the council reading, a multinational church is a visible sign to the powers that their claim on the nations is over.
5840: The nations healed and the sons of God restored
5841: In the new creation the kings of the earth bring the glory of the nations into the city, and the leaves of the tree of life are "for the healing of the nations". Believers, now "sons of God" by adoption (Rom 8:14-19; Gal 3:26), will judge angels and share Christ's throne. On the council reading, redeemed humans take the place in God's family once given to the failed sons of God; other interpreters describe the same texts as the restoration of humanity's original vocation to rule creation.
5843: No clear Genesis 10 counterpart; their homeland in north-east Iran lay beyond the peoples the Table names.
5844: Rome's great eastern rival in the first century; large Jewish communities lived in their empire, descended from the exiles. First in Luke's list, which runs roughly east to west.
5847: Centred on Ecbatana (Hamadan). Israelite exiles were settled "in the cities of the Medes" (2 Kgs 17:6).
5850: An ancient kingdom in south-west Iran around Susa. Elam had long ceased to exist as a state by Luke's day, which is one reason some scholars think Luke's list is modelled on older or biblical geography.
5852: Asshur and Arphaxad, sons of Shem (Gen 10:22); Nimrod's cities in Shinar, including Babel (Gen 10:10-11).
5853: The land of Babel itself, and of Abraham's origins at Ur; home of the large Babylonian Jewish community.
5855: The land of the Canaanite clans (Gen 10:15-19), later given to Abraham's descendants through Shem's line via Eber.
5856: Jerusalem is the starting point of the mission (Acts 1:8; Rom 15:19). Its inclusion in a list of foreign lands is a puzzle; some suggest it means greater Judea or is a scribal change.
5858: Josephus (*Antiquities* 1.6) linked the Cappadocians with Meshech, a son of Japheth (Gen 10:2); the identification is uncertain.
5859: Central Anatolia around Caesarea Mazaca (Kayseri). Addressed in 1 Pet 1:1.
5861: No secure Genesis 10 link; Josephus associated neighbouring Black Sea peoples with Riphath and Tiras (Gen 10:2-3).
5862: On the southern Black Sea coast; home of Aquila (Acts 18:2) and addressed in 1 Pet 1:1.
5864: Lud, a son of Shem (Gen 10:22), traditionally identified with the Lydians of western Anatolia.
5865: Western Anatolia, capital Ephesus, where Paul spent over two years so that "all the residents of Asia heard the word" (Acts 19:10). Home of the seven churches of Rev 2–3.
5867: Josephus linked Togarmah (Gen 10:3) with the Phrygians; uncertain.
5868: Inland Anatolia; Paul passed through "the region of Phrygia and Galatia" on his second and third journeys (Acts 16:6; Acts 18:23). Colossae and Laodicea lay in Phrygia.
5871: The southern Anatolian coastal plain; Paul and Barnabas landed at Perga, where John Mark left them (Acts 13:13; Acts 14:24-25).
5873: Alexandria had one of the largest Jewish communities in the world and produced the Septuagint. Apollos came from there (Acts 18:24). Isaiah foresaw an altar to Yahweh in Egypt (Isa 19:19-25).
5875: Put, a son of Ham (Gen 10:6), identified with Libya by Josephus and the Septuagint; also the Lehabim (Gen 10:13).
5876: Cyrene in modern eastern Libya had a large Jewish community; Simon who carried Jesus' cross came from there (Mark 15:21), and men of Cyrene first preached to Greeks at Antioch (Acts 11:20).
5877: No direct Genesis 10 entry; later Jewish interpretation sometimes applied Kittim (Gen 10:4) to Rome (compare Dan 11:30, which the Greek renders "Romans").
5878: "Visitors from Rome" heard Peter at Pentecost; a church existed there before Paul arrived as a prisoner (Acts 28:14-16; Rom 1:7). Acts ends with Paul preaching there unhindered.
5880: Caphtorim (Gen 10:14), usually identified with Crete (compare Amos 9:7; Jer 47:4).
5881: Paul's ship sheltered at Fair Havens on Crete (Acts 27:7-13); Titus was left there to organise churches (Titus 1:5), implying a later visit.
5883: The sons of Joktan, such as Sheba and Havilah (Gen 10:26-30), and Cush's sons Seba and Dedan (Gen 10:7).
5884: Probably the Nabataean kingdom (capital Petra), south and east of Judea. Paul went "away into Arabia" after his conversion (Gal 1:17); what he did there is not stated.
5887: Most scholars identify Tarshish with Tartessos in south-west Spain (near Huelva), though Sardinia and Tarsus have also been proposed. It was the farthest west Jonah could flee (Jonah 1:3) and is named in Isa 66:19 among the far nations. Paul planned to go to Spain (Rom 15:24, 28); whether he did is uncertain (1 Clement 5.7 says he reached "the limit of the west").
5889: No clear Genesis 10 counterpart; it lay in the regions later Jewish geography gave to Japheth.
5890: The Roman province along the eastern Adriatic (roughly modern Albania to Croatia). Paul says he preached "as far as Illyricum" (Rom 15:19); whether he entered it or reached its border from Macedonia is debated. 2 Tim 4:10 mentions Titus going to Dalmatia, part of it.
5892: Kittim (Gen 10:4) in one line of interpretation: 1 Maccabees 1:1 says Alexander came from "the land of Kittim".
5893: Entered after the vision of the man of Macedonia (Acts 16:9-10); churches at Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea. The first recorded church in Europe.
5895: Javan (Gen 10:2), the Ionian Greeks; Elishah (Gen 10:4) is also sometimes placed in Greece.
5896: Southern Greece, capital Corinth, where Paul stayed eighteen months (Acts 18:11); also Athens (Acts 17:16-34).
5898: Gomer, son of Japheth (Gen 10:2), whom Josephus identified with the Galatians (Gauls).
5899: Central Anatolia (capital Ancyra/Ankara); the Roman province also included Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. Paul wrote Galatians to churches there; whether north or south Galatia is meant is debated.
5901: Kittim, son of Javan (Gen 10:4), named after Kition on Cyprus; Elishah may also be Cyprus (Alashiya).
5902: Barnabas's home (Acts 4:36) and the first stop of the first journey, from Salamis to Paphos, where the proconsul Sergius Paulus believed (Acts 13:4-12).
5904: Josephus linked Tarshish (Gen 10:4) with Tarsus; most modern scholars prefer a western site for Tarshish.
5905: Paul's home city (Acts 21:39; Acts 22:3); he worked in "Syria and Cilicia" for years before the recorded journeys (Gal 1:21).
5908: The Nubian kingdom of Meroë on the upper Nile, south of Egypt. The gospel reached it through the Ethiopian official baptised by Philip (Acts 8:26-39), whom some read as fulfilling Ps 68:31.
5909: Isn't a divine council just polytheism?
5910: Council readers say no. Polytheism means worshipping many gods who share power and often have their own origins. In the Bible the council members are created (Neh 9:6; Ps 148:2-5; Col 1:16), owe Yahweh worship (Ps 29:1-2; Ps 97:7), can be judged and sentenced to die (Ps 82:7), and Israel may worship none of them (Exod 20:3). Yahweh is unique in kind: the only uncreated one, the Creator of the rest. Heiser summed it up as "Yahweh is an elohim, but no other elohim is Yahweh"; scholars often use terms like "monolatry" (worship of one God) or speak of Yahweh's "incomparability".
5911: Classical theists agree the Bible forbids worship of other beings but prefer to call the council members "angels" and avoid the word "gods" except for idols or as figurative language, worried that loose talk of "gods" blurs the Creator–creature line. Historical critics such as Mark Smith argue that some older texts (e.g. Deut 32:8-9 in its older form, Ps 82) do reflect a real early Israelite polytheism or henotheism, which later writers reinterpreted. Nathan MacDonald argues that "monotheism" (a 17th-century term) is a poor label for Deuteronomy, whose concern is exclusive loyalty to Yahweh, not abstract counting of gods.
5912: Doesn't the Shema say there is only one God?
5913: The Shema (Deut 6:4) can be translated "Yahweh our God, Yahweh is one" or "Yahweh is our God, Yahweh alone." Many scholars think its main point is exclusive loyalty: Israel must love Yahweh alone with all its heart (Deut 6:5). The same book says Yahweh is "God of gods" (Deut 10:17) and warns against serving other gods (Deut 6:14), and also says "there is no other besides him" (Deut 4:35, 39). Council readers take these together as saying Yahweh is unique and supreme, not that no other spiritual beings exist.
5914: Jewish and Christian tradition has long read the Shema as a confession of the oneness of God, and many scholars read Deut 4:35, 39 as a clear denial that other gods are real gods at all. Christians also note that Paul rewrites the Shema to include Jesus (1 Cor 8:6), which Bauckham calls "christological monotheism". Critical scholars often think Deut 4 is a later (exilic) layer that moves toward stricter monotheism than the earlier chapters.
5915: What about "there is no god besides me" in Isaiah?
5916: Isaiah 40–48 repeatedly says "there is no other" and "besides me there is no god" (Isa 45:5; 46:9). Council readers note that Babylon says almost the same words of herself, "I am, and there is no one besides me" (Isa 47:8, 10), and so does Nineveh (Zeph 2:15). Babylon did not mean no other cities existed; she meant none could compare. So, they argue, the phrase is a claim of incomparability: no other being is like Yahweh in power, knowledge of the future or ability to save.
5917: Many scholars read Second Isaiah as the Bible's first explicit, theoretical monotheism: the idols are "nothing" (Isa 41:24, 29), made from half a log used for firewood (Isa 44:9-20), and "before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me" (Isa 43:10). On this view the comparison with Isa 47:8 shows the same boast, but the context makes Yahweh's claim stronger. Some suggest a middle way: Isaiah denies that any other being is truly "god" in the sense of creator and saviour, while not denying heavenly beings exist.
5918: Aren't the "gods" of Psalm 82 just human judges?
5919: Most modern commentators think not. The psalm sets the scene in "the council of El", contrasts the gods with humans ("you will die like men" and "fall like any prince"), and ends by asking God to judge "the earth" and inherit "all the nations", which fits beings with authority over nations, not Israelite magistrates. Hans-Joachim Kraus's Psalms commentary, for example, rejects the human-judges view. Divine beings held responsible for justice on earth also fits Isa 24:21 and Dan 10.
5920: The human-judges view has a long history among Jewish and Christian interpreters (including Calvin and many Puritans) and is still held by some evangelical scholars. Its supporters point to texts where elohim may mean judges (Exod 21:6; Exod 22:8-9), to the purely human sins named (partiality, neglect of orphans), and to Jesus' comment that those "to whom the word of God came" were called gods (John 10:35), which seems to describe humans. Others read the psalm as addressed to Israel at Sinai, or to foreign kings who claimed divinity.
